In November 2017, Dunham and her creative partner Jenni Konner defended *Girls* writer [Murray Miller](/wiki/Murray_Miller "Murray Miller"), whom actress [Aurora Perrineau](/wiki/Aurora_Perrineau "Aurora Perrineau") had accused of sexually assaulting her in 2012, posting a statement that said, "While our first instinct is to listen to every woman's story, our insider knowledge of Murray's situation makes us confident that sadly this accusation is one of the 3% of assault cases that are misreported every year."[[147]](#cite_note-BBC-147) Dunham was described as a "[hipster racist](/wiki/Hipster_racist "Hipster racist")" for her defense of Miller, as Perrineau is of mixed race.[[148]](#cite_note-148) In December 2018, Dunham wrote a letter of apology to Perrineau and stated that, contrary to her statement, she had no "insider information" that exonerated Murray.[[149]](#cite_note-149)[[150]](#cite_note-150) In her 2026 memoir *Famesick*, Dunham stated that she issued the statement shortly after her hysterectomy while high on pain medication, and called it the one thing in her life about which she feels "genuine shame".[[151]](#cite_note-151)[[121]](#cite_note-:0-121)

In December 2016, Dunham observed on her podcast, Women of the Hour, that she never had an [abortion](/wiki/Abortion "Abortion"), but wished she had, so as to better understand women who have experienced it. The comment was widely condemned as insensitive and distasteful.[[152]](#cite_note-152)[[153]](#cite_note-153) Dunham later issued a lengthy apology on her [Instagram](/wiki/Instagram "Instagram").[[154]](#cite_note-154)
